text:
maria: Heads-up, ran a Karpenter experiment in us-west-2 yesterday to test cross-zone provisioning for our GPU job burst pattern. Short thread with logs + config.
jon: Nice — what was the failure mode you were seeing?
arjun: TL;DR: pods stuck Pending because one AZ hit ENI and instance-type limits, and Karpenter kept trying new AZs until TTL expired.
lisa: Oof. Did Karpenter not fall back to our on-demand gpu nodepool? maria: It did not — we had a provisioner with ttlSecondsUntilExpired: 300 and consolidation enabled; Karpenter attempted multiple instance types across zones and then gave up. We expected the fallback-policy to route to nodepool, but our taints/tolerations didn't match.
jon: Can you paste the provisioner yaml you used? curious about topologySpread and constraints.
maria: Sure, snippet below:
```
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1alpha5
kind: Provisioner
metadata:
  name: gpu-burst-provisioner
spec:
  ttlSecondsUntilExpired: 300
  consolidate: true
  requirements:
    - key: kubernetes.io/arch
      operator: In
      values: [amd64]
    - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      operator: In
      values: [us-west-2a,us-west-2b,us-west-2c]
  provider:
    instanceProfile: arn:aws:iam::111111111111:instance-profile/infra-node
    subnetSelector:
      karpenter.sh/discovery: us-west-2
    securityGroupSelector:
      ka: default
  limits:
    resources:
      cpu: 2000
      memory: 8192Gi
      pods: 2000
```
arjun: I see — no explicit instance type list and no spot/ondemand preference. Karpenter will try any compatible type; with GPUs that means p3/p4/g5 etc and AZs have different capacities.
lisa: Do we have ENI limits per AZ hitting us? our cluster ENI quota is global but per-AZ instance count matters.
maria: On the logs we hit this error from the AWS API: "InsufficientInstanceCapacity: Not enough capacity in the requested Availability Zone." Then we saw errors like "AttachNetworkInterface limit exceeded" for a few instance types.
jon: That suggests two orthogonal issues: (1) AZ-specific spare GPU capacity, (2) VPC ENI limits from many small instances. For bursty GPU workloads, bin-packing onto fewer bigger instances (fewer ENIs) helps.
arjun: Agreed. We tested another run where we constrained instanceTypes to [p4d.24xlarge,p4de.24xlarge] and set provider.spot: true and overprovisioning: true. Karpenter still launched in one AZ; but TTL was reduced to 60 in that test so it was quicker but still sometimes failed.
lisa: What about setting ttlSecondsUntilExpired to something longer so Karpenter retries across AZs? Tradeoff is cold pod latency and cost for long-lived unused nodes.
maria: Exactly the tradeoff we discussed. Also consolidation sometimes deletes nodes before pods finished warming up (model cache), causing extra cold-starts.
jon: Have we considered a hybrid policy: allow Karpenter to provision for up to X seconds, then if unscheduled pods remain, shift those to a reserved gpu-nodepool via a mutating webhook or by setting a pod annotation that matches nodepool tolerations?
arjun: We prototyped a controller that watches unscheduled GPU pods > 45s and copies them with nodeSelector gpu-reserved=true. Works but messy.
lisa: Could we instead use Karpenter's provisioner.kubeletConfiguration or labels to prefer packing into larger instance types by using predicted resource requests? e.g., require node.kubernetes.io/instance-type in requirements with a list of large GPUs.
maria: We also discovered podTopologySpread was allowing pods to scatter evenly across AZs which increased ENI usage. For bursts, we want pack-first strategy.
jon: Option list:
- Increase ttlSecondsUntilExpired to 900 and accept slower failure recovery.
- Add explicit instanceType list biased to large multi-GPU instances to reduce ENI count.
- Disable topologySpread for batch GPU jobs via Label + PodPreset.
- Implement controller to reannotate stuck pods to reserved nodepool after N sec.
- Use Karpenter fallback: set provisioner.spec.constraints to avoid certain AZs and have nodepool in those AZs so scheduler will schedule there when Karpenter can't.

arjun: Also monitor metrics: NodeStartupLatency, ProvisioningFailures, PodPendingDuration. We ran a PromQL for last test:
```
max_over_time(karpenter_provisioner_provisioning_latency_seconds[10m])
```
maria: Results: median provisioning ~ 70s when available, 5m+ when capacity exhausted as Karpenter retries. Cost-wise, using larger instances reduced token-per-GPU cost by ~18% because fewer nodes = less baseline overhead.
lisa: Any network workaround? e.g., use ENI Trunking (aws-cni with trunk support)? That reduces ENI pressure but we already enabled trunking on the cluster.
jon: Another angle: keep a small warm pool of large GPU nodes in each AZ (1 per AZ) as a safety net for bursts — that increases baseline cost but gives predictable latency and avoids ENI spikes.
arjun: I think for prod we should combine: reserve 1 warm large node per AZ + Karpenter for scaling beyond that, set ttlSecondsUntilExpired=600, constrain instance types to big GPUs, and disable topologySpread for batch training jobs.
maria: Agreed. I'll prep a runbook with these steps and a canary plan. Quick checklist:
- [ ] Update provisioner constraints to prefer large types
- [ ] Set ttlSecondsUntilExpired: 600
- [ ] Add pod label gpu.pack.strategy=pack and mutating webhook to translate to topologySpreadPolicy=\"Pack\"
- [ ] Keep 1 warm large GPU node per AZ in nodepool
- [ ] Dashboard alerts for provisioning failures > 3 in 10m
- [ ] Cost impact estimate for warm nodes

lisa: Ping me when you have the runbook, I'll review the webhook code.
sre-bot: Incident created: #INC-2026 - Karpenter GPU provisioning flakiness (linked to thread 1771001123)
jon: Thanks maria — solid notes. If you want I can help with the cost calc and Grafana panels.
maria: Thanks — will assign tasks in the runbook. Closing the experiment thread, will open a PR with config changes next week. :rocket:
